questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
When choosing Milan as my study destination, the potential for cultural experience and personal growth played a pivotal role in my decision.

Milan, as a global hub of art, fashion, and design, offered an unparalleled opportunity to immerse myself in a culture rich in history and creativity. From exploring iconic landmarks like the Duomo and The Last Supper to engaging with the vibrant local traditions, I knew that living in Milan would deepen my appreciation for Italian heritage. The city's dynamic blend of modernity and tradition provided countless opportunities to learn, connect, and experience life in a truly cosmopolitan environment.

On a personal level, studying in Milan promised significant growth. Living in a bustling international city challenged me to adapt to new environments, embrace cultural differences, and build independence. Navigating daily life in a new country, whether learning Italian phrases or understanding local customs, helped me develop resilience, flexibility, and a more global perspective.

Milan was not just a place to study - it was a transformative experience that enriched my worldview and shaped me both personally and culturally.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Future exchange students living off-campus in Milan should keep the following in mind:

Accommodation Options: Platforms like Spotahome, HousingAnywhere, or local Facebook groups can help you find housing. Start your search early, as demand for student housing is high.

Location Matters: Consider proximity to public transport and your university. Milan has an efficient metro and tram system, so being near a station can make commuting much easier.

Costs and Deposits: Be prepared for higher rent prices compared to other cities, especially in central areas. Most landlords require a deposit, so budget accordingly.

Neighborhood Vibe: Explore different neighborhoods before deciding. Areas like Navigli and Brera offer vibrant atmospheres, while quieter areas like Bicocca may suit those looking for a calmer environment.

Community Connection: Living off-campus can feel isolating at times, so make an effort to join university groups, WhatsApp networks, or Erasmus meetups to stay connected and socialize.

Also remember to register an Italian TAX-code though the government by email, since you will need that to book housing.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not very succesful. Many of my pre-approved courses were unavailable, so I had to go through the process of obtaining new pre-approvals and updating my Online Learning Agreement. However, registering courses on the UniMi website was straightforward since you simply enter the course details manually.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Finding available courses can be a challenging process. Even after selecting your courses, one or more may become unavailable once the term starts. Additionally, ensuring that your chosen courses fit into a schedule without overlaps can be difficult, often requiring further adjustments and changes. However, the option to register as either attending or non-attending can provide more flexibility, making it easier to manage overlaps and accommodate your schedule.

questions.answer: I was surprised to find that there were no mandatory readings for each class, only for the exam. Otherwise, attending the classes was easy, though at times the Italian accent made it a bit challenging to fully understand.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching style varied across courses. Some classes were more interactive, encouraging participation and discussion, while others followed a more traditional, PowerPoint-style approach. Regarding group work, I had one course that included a group presentation as part of the exam. Some classes fostered more inclusive and engaging environments, while others were more focused on lectures and slides.

questions.answer: I attended the following courses on MA-levels: Journalism, Media and Politict (9 ects), Digital Society (9 ects), Corporate Communication (9 ects) and a Workshop in Iconology and Iconography (3 ects).

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I highly recommend the Workshop in Iconology and Iconography for exchange students interested in art history. The professor was exceptionally knowledgeable and an excellent teacher, and the course included fascinating excursions. Additionally, when in Italy, taking art courses is a must—it’s the heart of art history, offering unparalleled opportunities to study masterpieces in their cultural context.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Milan is a city full of exciting opportunities to explore, relax, and immerse yourself in Italian culture. Here’s a guide to help you make the most of your weekends and holidays:

1. Restaurants to Try
Dongio: A quiet spot for reasonably priced Italian dishes paired with good wine.
Osteria Serafina: Indulge in a luxurious experience—try their famous pasta prepared in a giant parmesan wheel. (Remember to book in advance!)
Rovello 18 and Tram Tram: Both offer authentic Italian cuisine in cozy settings.
Osteria di Fortunata: Located in the trendy Brera district, this chain serves delicious handmade pasta.
Il Brutto: Perfect for weekday lunches with a menu that changes bi-weekly.

2. Cafés for a Relaxing Break
Gelsomina: A charming café with Italian decor
Breaddy Bakery: A budget-friendly spot for brunch, lunch, or a hearty lasagna.
Loste Café: A Milanese take on Copenhagen-style cafés, featuring excellent pastries.
Crazy Cat Café: A quirky spot where you can enjoy brunch or aperitivo while spending time with friendly cats. They also host fun events like drag bingo!
Panificio Davide Longoni: Savor their focaccia or a ham sandwich with Dijon mustard.
Signor Lievito: The place to go if you’re craving cardamom buns or cinnamon rolls.
3. Must-See Museums
Palazzo Reale: Visit for rotating exhibitions on art and history.
The Last Supper Museum: See Leonardo da Vinci’s masterpiece, but be sure to book tickets at least two months in advance.
Pinacoteca di Brera: Milan’s answer to the Louvre, with an impressive collection of Renaissance art.
Villa Necchi: Step into a 1930s Italian villa, a preserved time capsule of luxury living.
4. Other Landmarks and Activities
Duomo Milano: Climb to the rooftop for breathtaking views of the city.
Teatro La Scala: Attend an opera or simply tour this historic theater.
Bagni Misterioso: If it’s summer, cool off at this outdoor pool, which also offers food and drinks.

5. Parks for Relaxation
Parco Sempione: A large and beautiful park, perfect for picnics or leisurely walks.
Giardini Indro Montanelli: A romantic park with fountains and a smaller castle—great for dog lovers!

6. Shopping Spots
Calzedonia: Stock up on stylish tights and leggings.
REHUB or Humana Vintage: Explore these vintage stores for unique finds.
East Market Shop: A treasure trove of retro clothing.

7. Bars and Nightlife
Rizla: Budget-friendly and potent drinks for just €3.50.
De Amicis Uno: A must for aperitivo fans; enjoy an Aperol Spritz with a generous snack platter.
Trattoir La Darsensa: Known as the "Danish Bar," this lively spot offers a mix of live music, dancing, and good vibes on weekends.
Alcatraz: A massive dance club with performances that make for an unforgettable night out.
Bar Basso: Allegedly the birthplace of the negroni sbagliato. They serve these iconic cocktails in generous portions.
Tempio del Futuro Perduto: A techno club with an industrial vibe, perfect for fans of electronic music. It’s a go-to destination for late-night dancing on weekends.
King’s Pub: A lively bar with an international crowd. Known for its fun and interactive vibe, it hosts beer pong nights every Thursday, making it a great place to meet new people and enjoy a laid-back evening.

8. Markets to Explore
San Marco (Monday and Thursday) or Fauché (Saturday): Browse for fresh produce, snacks, or unique souvenirs.
Porta Romana (Friday): Perfect for a relaxed morning of market shopping.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the local culture in Milan was a smooth, albeit gradual, process. As a cosmopolitan city, Milan blends traditional Italian culture with international influences. The people were warm and welcoming, and I found that participating in daily activities—whether it was ordering coffee at a café or shopping at the local market—helped me get in tune with the city's pace. Since Italians generally prefer speaking Italian, learning some basic phrases proved to be incredibly useful for navigating everyday life.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: One of the cultural differences I found particularly challenging was the slower pace of life compared to what I was used to. The slower response times in emails, the more relaxed attitude towards deadlines, and people strolling slowly on the streets were initially a bit frustrating. However, over time, I adjusted and learned to embrace the more laid-back rhythm of life.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I most appreciated the Italian emphasis on enjoying life and savoring the moment. The long, leisurely meals and coffee breaks were a highlight for me, as they encouraged not only relaxation but also meaningful social interactions. The Italian approach to food was another aspect I loved—the focus on fresh, high-quality ingredients and the joy of sharing meals with friends really resonated with me.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be Patient and Adapt to the Pace: Milan has a more relaxed pace of life compared to what you might be used to at UCPH. Things like response times, deadlines, and even the general rhythm of daily life can be slower, so it’s important to be patient and flexible. Don’t rush—embrace the slower pace and enjoy the moments, whether it's a long meal or a coffee break.

Explore Milan and Beyond: Milan is a dynamic city with a mix of modern and historical attractions. Take time to explore the neighborhoods, art, museums, and nearby cities. Milan's public transport makes it easy to travel, so don’t miss the chance to visit other parts of Italy or even nearby countries on weekends.

Stay Open to New Experiences: There will be many opportunities to get involved in cultural activities, events, and social gatherings—whether organized by the university or local groups. Stay open to new experiences, even if they are outside your comfort zone. These events, from local festivals to student meetups, will help you integrate, meet new people, and enrich your time abroad.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Yes, I think a useful tip would be to learn some useful italian phrases (either on Duolingo or join an Italian course). Simple greetings, ordering food, or asking for directions in Italian can help you feel more integrated and appreciated by locals.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was definitely the opportunity to be on my own and gain new confidence. Living in a new city, navigating daily life, and handling challenges independently helped me grow in ways I hadn't expected, even though at times it was rather stressfull. Beyond the cultural and academic experiences, the sense of self-assurance I gained from managing everything on my own was truly invaluable. This newfound confidence is something I’ll carry with me for years to come.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge during my exchange was adjusting to the slower pace of life in Milan. While it can be refreshing, the slower pace sometimes made everyday tasks, like dealing with bureaucratic processes or waiting for responses, feel frustratingly drawn out.
